Mendacious means deliberately lying. A mendacious person is someone who tells falsehoods not by mistake, not out of confusion, but knowingly and on purpose. A mendacious statement is one that is false and was crafted to deceive.

The heart of this word is intent. This is critical.

If someone gives you wrong information because they themselves believed it to be true, they are not being mendacious — they are simply mistaken. Mendacious only applies when a person knows the truth and consciously chooses to say something false. It is lying, not error.

Mendacious can describe a person, a statement, or a pattern of behavior.

A person: "He was a mendacious con artist who lied to everyone he met."

A statement or claim: "The report was packed with mendacious claims designed to mislead the public."

A pattern: "Her mendacious behavior eventually cost her every friendship she had."

When used to describe a person, it usually implies they lie habitually — as a character trait — not just on a single occasion.

Mendacious is a strong, serious word — it is a clear and deliberate accusation. It is sharper and heavier than simply saying someone is "not fully honest" or "a bit misleading." When you call someone or something mendacious, you are stating plainly: this is a lie, and it was told on purpose.

This is a formal word. You will find it most in:

  • Political commentary and journalism
  • Legal and professional writing
  • Essays, editorials, and literature

In everyday casual conversation, people are far more likely to say "he's a liar" than "he's mendacious" — though both carry the same meaning. Mendacious simply sounds more measured, precise, and serious. It is the word you reach for when you want to make a pointed, formal accusation without sounding reckless or emotional.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Placing mendacious among related words sharpens your understanding of exactly where it sits:

Lying — the most blunt and everyday version. Direct. Plain. No frills.

Dishonest — broader than mendacious. A dishonest person may cheat, manipulate, or steal — not just tell lies.

Deceitful — similar to mendacious, but includes trickery and manipulation that goes beyond spoken or written falsehoods.

Untruthful — softer and more neutral. It doesn't carry the same strong implication of deliberate, harmful intent.

Duplicitous — implies being two-faced; saying one thing while hiding a completely different agenda.

Mendacious sits squarely in the zone of deliberate, knowing, intentional falsehood — usually in a formal context.

1. "The mendacious salesman promised results he knew the product could never deliver."
  2. "Her mendacious account of events was completely dismantled by video footage."
  3. "Voters grew increasingly frustrated with the candidate's mendacious promises."
  4. "Lying came so naturally to him that even those close to him described him as deeply mendacious."
  5. "The autobiography was later exposed as largely mendacious, having invented many of the events it described."

The noun form is mendacity, meaning the quality or habit of being mendacious — essentially, habitual lying. Example: "The mendacity of his testimony left the courtroom stunned." You'll see these two words — mendacious and mendacity — traveling together frequently.
Mendacious = deliberately and knowingly untruthful. It is a formal, strong word used to describe a person who lies on purpose, or a statement that is intentionally false.
